group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 74-year-old woman presented this morning to the peri-operative medicine clinic for evaluation in advance of next week’s elective two-level lumbar laminectomy with posterolateral fusion planned for symptomatic spinal stenosis at L4-L5 and L5-S1 that has limited her to walking half a block with a cane before numbness radiates down both calves; the procedure will be performed through a midline posterior approach under general anesthesia with an anticipated operative time of approximately 150 minutes and an overnight stay on the orthopedic ward; this musculoskeletal operation is outside the intrathoracic, intraperitoneal, or suprainguinal vascular categories and is therefore not considered high risk for major cardiac events. She arrived seated comfortably, transferred to the examination table without assistance, and reported that outside of her neurogenic claudication she remains capable of tending her small backyard garden, cooking daily meals, and ascending the eight steps to her porch while carrying groceries without shortness of breath, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, or ankle swelling. Five years ago she experienced a left hemispheric lacunar infarct manifested by transient right facial droop and arm weakness that resolved completely over subsequent weeks; she was subsequently placed on aspirin 81 mg daily and high-intensity atorvastatin, has followed with neurology annually, and denies any recurrent focal neurologic symptoms, speech difficulty, vision loss, or carotid bruit on prior examinations. Her chronic medical conditions include well-controlled essential hypertension diagnosed in her early sixties and treated with amlodipine 5 mg each morning, diet-managed type 2 diabetes mellitus first noted on routine screening three years ago with a hemoglobin A1c of 6.4 % last month on metformin 500 mg twice daily, stage 2 chronic kidney disease attributed to long-standing vascular risk factors, osteoarthritis of both thumbs, and osteoporosis treated with weekly oral alendronate; she has never required insulin therapy. She has never been hospitalized for fluid overload or required loop diuretics, has not noticed nocturnal cough or weight gain, and states that recent transthoracic echocardiography obtained during a hypertension workup revealed normal chamber sizes and an ejection fraction of 60 %; she has no prior diagnosis of congestive heart failure or cardiomyopathy. She never smoked cigarettes, drinks a single glass of wine on holidays only, and denies illicit drug use. Family history is notable for a brother who underwent carotid endarterectomy at 70 and a mother with late-onset Alzheimer disease; there is no premature cardiac death among first-degree relatives. Current medications also include lisinopril 10 mg daily, cholecalciferol 2000 IU daily, and calcium carbonate with the evening meal; she reports no medication allergies. Review of systems is negative for chest pressure with exertion, palpitations, syncope, claudication, abdominal pain, or weight loss. On physical examination she appears alert, relaxed, and oriented. Vital signs after five minutes seated rest show blood pressure 124/66 mm Hg in the right arm, heart rate 62 beats/min in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 99 % breathing ambient air, and oral temperature 36.6 °C; body mass index is 27 kg/m². Jugular venous pulsation is not elevated, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, and auscultation reveals a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or extra sounds. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout with good excursion. Abdomen is soft and nontender with no hepatosplenomegaly or pulsatile masses. Distal pulses are 2+ and symmetric, and there is no pedal edema. Neurologic examination demonstrates intact cranial nerves, normal strength in all extremities, symmetric reflexes, and steady gait with a cane. Lumbar palpation elicits midline tenderness at L4–L5 without step-off, and straight-leg raise reproduces bilateral posterior thigh pain. Pre-operative laboratory testing obtained one hour before the visit shows hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, white blood cell count 6.1 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 228 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 1.35 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 52 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting glucose this morning was 118 mg/dL, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol 68 mg/dL, and liver function tests are within reference limits. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram performed today reveals normal sinus rhythm at 60 beats/min, normal intervals, and no ST-T wave abnormalities. Upright anteroposterior and lateral chest radiographs demonstrate clear lung fields and a normal cardiac silhouette. Airway evaluation shows a Mallampati class II oropharynx with full cervical extension, interincisor distance of 4 cm, and intact dentition. She has been counseled to continue her antihypertensive agents and aspirin through the morning of surgery, to take her usual metformin dose the day prior but withhold it the morning of the procedure, and to maintain clear liquids up until two hours before anesthesia induction. The spine surgeon reviewed operative details, need for prone positioning, potential for neurophysiologic monitoring, and risks including infection, dural tear, neurologic deficit, venous thromboembolism, and myocardial events; the anesthesia team plans standard monitors without arterial line and will target euvolemia to protect renal function. After a thorough discussion, the patient verbalized understanding, asked pertinent questions about postoperative rehabilitation and pain control with multimodal analgesia, and expressed eagerness to proceed in hopes of returning to longer walks and gardening without leg pain.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative criteria:
• High-risk surgery: lumbar fusion is not intrathoracic, intraperitoneal, or suprainguinal vascular surgery, 0.
• Ischemic heart disease: no history or evidence reported, 0.
• Congestive heart failure: no history or clinical findings, 0.
• Cerebrovascular disease: prior lacunar infarct, +1 even though the deficits resolved.
• Diabetes treated with insulin: metformin only, 0.
• Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: preoperative creatinine 1.35 mg/dL, 0.
Total = 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 1.
Final answer: 1
